title: AlexNet, 2012: what actually changed was GPUs and ImageNet
story:
The architecture was not new and it was not obscure. LeCun, Bottou, Bengio and Haffner published Gradient-based learning applied to document recognition in the Proceedings of the IEEE in November 1998, describing convolutional networks trained by gradient descent and applied to reading handwritten documents in commercial use. That is fourteen years of the idea being available, published in a flagship venue, and working in production on a real task.

Then at the 2012 ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge, the network designed by Alex Krizhevsky with Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton, his doctoral advisor, reached a top-five error rate of 15.3% against 26.2% for the second-best entry — which used a conventional pipeline of hand-crafted features and a linear classifier. The task was classifying 1.2 million high-resolution images into 1,000 classes. A margin of nearly eleven points in a competition where progress had been arriving in fractions of a point is not an improvement; it is a different answer to the question of what the field should be doing.

The usual summary is that nothing mathematical changed and only scale did. That is mostly right and it is worth getting exactly right, because one of the four ingredients people list does not belong in the old column.

What was genuinely old: the convolutional architecture, gradient descent, and the dataset. Deng, Dong, Socher, Li, Li and Fei-Fei presented ImageNet at CVPR in 2009, three years before the network that made it famous — so the data was sitting there, published, waiting.

What was not old is dropout. It was introduced in Improving neural networks by preventing co-adaptation of feature detectors, submitted on 3 July 2012 by Hinton, Srivastava, Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Salakhutdinov — months before the December conference paper, and sharing three of its five authors. So dropout is not a technique the network reached for from the shelf; it is a technique from the same people at the same time, and the honest version of the thesis has to say so. Its idea is that overfitting in a large network trained on a small set is greatly reduced by randomly omitting half of the feature detectors on each training case, which prevents co-adaptations in which a detector is only useful alongside several specific others, so each neuron has to learn a generally useful feature.

The compute half of the story deserves its specifics, because they are humbler than the legend. The network has five convolutional layers and 60 million parameters, and one forward pass takes roughly 1.1 billion multiply-accumulate operations. It was trained for five to six days on two NVIDIA GeForce GTX 580 3GB cards — consumer graphics hardware — with the layers divided between the two because the model did not fit on one. The division was not a parallelism strategy chosen for elegance. It was a workaround for a card that was too small.

One more correction to the story as usually told: the winning submission was not a single network. It averaged the predictions of several similar networks together with a variant pre-trained on the larger autumn 2011 release of the data. The thing that won the competition was an ensemble, which is worth knowing before quoting the margin as a property of one architecture.

So the accurate summary is narrower and more useful than the slogan. An architecture that had been published for fourteen years became decisively better than the alternatives when a dataset of unprecedented size met hardware cheap enough for a graduate student to own two of — with one genuinely new regularisation idea, produced by the same group, doing part of the work.

problem.name: Waiting on inputs, not on ideas
problem.shape: A published approach is not competitive, and the reason may be its inputs rather than its design.
tell: the method was tried, performed poorly, and was concluded to be a dead end
its performance improves whenever data or compute increase
the competitive alternatives rely on hand-built components
nobody has re-run it at the scale now available
problem.move: Before concluding an approach does not work, establish what it was given. Separate the claim 'this design is wrong' from 'this design was starved', and check whether its results improved with data and compute — because if they did, the experiment that matters is the one nobody has run yet.
problem.invariant: An approach whose performance scales with its inputs cannot be evaluated at a fixed input size. What looks like a property of the method may be a property of the budget it was tested under.
problem.breaks: The reading is applied retrospectively to a case that succeeded, which makes it look more decisive than it was. The winning submission was an ensemble including a network pre-trained on a larger data release, one of its four ingredients was months old rather than years, and a great many approaches that scaled with compute have not become competitive by waiting. Selecting the case that worked is not evidence that waiting is a strategy.

cost.time: five to six days of training per run, in an era when that was the whole iteration loop
cost.space: a model that did not fit on one card, so layers were split across two by hand
cost.beats: hand-crafted features with a linear classifier, which were interpretable and had guarantees and had stopped improving, and simply building a bigger hand-engineered pipeline, which is what the runner-up did

worked.problem: Why did the 2012 result land when the convolutional architecture had already been published and deployed in 1998?
worked.reasoning:
Because the architecture had never been given a dataset or a compute budget of that size, and this particular family of method is one whose performance is a function of exactly those two things. The 1998 result is not a weaker version of the 2012 one; it is the same idea evaluated under a budget that could not reveal what it was capable of.

Put the numbers next to each other, because they are what make the argument rather than decorate it. The 2012 task was classifying 1.2 million high-resolution images into 1,000 classes. The result was a top-five error rate of 15.3% against 26.2% for the second-best entry, which used a conventional pipeline of hand-crafted features and a linear classifier. Nearly eleven points, in a competition where progress had been arriving in fractions of a point. That is not an improvement within a paradigm, it is a verdict on the paradigm.

The dataset was not built for it and was not new. ImageNet was presented at CVPR in 2009, three years earlier, by Deng, Dong, Socher, Li, Li and Fei-Fei. The data was published and sitting there. The compute was consumer hardware: five to six days on two graphics cards with three gigabytes each, with the layers divided between them because sixty million parameters did not fit on one. That division was a workaround, not a parallelism strategy.

Now the correction I would insist on, because the usual telling overstates the thesis in a way that makes it less interesting. People list four old ingredients — convolutions, gradient descent, rectified activations, dropout — and conclude nothing mathematical changed. Dropout does not belong on that list. It was introduced in a paper submitted in July 2012, months before the December conference paper, by an author set overlapping in three of five names. Dropout is not a technique taken from the shelf; it came from the same people at the same time. So the accurate claim is that most of what was needed was old and one genuinely new regularisation idea was doing part of the work.

And a second correction, because the margin gets attributed to a single architecture: the winning submission averaged several similar networks together with a variant pre-trained on a larger release of the data. What won was an ensemble.

The general lesson is the part worth carrying, stated carefully. An approach whose performance scales with its inputs cannot be assessed at a fixed input size, so 'we tried it and it did not work' is an incomplete sentence without 'with this much data and this much compute'. The failure mode in 1998 through 2011 was not that anyone measured badly; it was concluding from a correct measurement at one scale that the design was wrong.

The limit on that lesson should be stated too, since it is easy to turn into an excuse. This case is selected because it succeeded. Plenty of approaches that scale with compute have not become competitive by waiting, and 'it will work at scale' is unfalsifiable until somebody runs it. The discipline the story actually supports is narrower: check whether results improved with inputs, and if they did, treat the untried scale as an open question rather than a closed one.

problem.practice: Find a result in your own area that was dismissed on measured evidence at a smaller scale than is now routine. Then work out what it would cost to re-run today, and whether the original conclusion was about the design or about the budget.

beats.broke: The architecture had been published and deployed more than a decade earlier and was not competitive, so the field concluded the approach was a dead end rather than an approach starved of inputs.
beats.fix: The inputs arrived — a labelled dataset of a size nobody had had, and consumer graphics cards programmable enough to train on it — and the same family of architecture won by a margin that ended the argument.
beats.cost: The winning result was an ensemble, trained for days on hardware split by hand because the model did not fit, and it traded the guarantees of the methods it displaced for empirical tuning.

interview.q: Why did the 2012 result land when the convolutional architecture had already been published and deployed in 1998?
interview.trap: Attributing the win to a new architecture or new mathematics. Most of what was needed was already published — but the opposite overcorrection is also wrong, because dropout was months old and came from the same group.

takeaway: An architecture published in 1998 and already running in production won by nearly eleven points in 2012 once a dataset published in 2009 met two consumer graphics cards — so the field's fourteen-year dismissal was a correct measurement at the wrong scale, though the honest version admits dropout was months old, from the same group, and that what won was an ensemble.
